title: Edible and Medicinal Mushrooms in Southeast Asia: Traditional Uses and Evidence Relevant to Mood, Cognition and Fatigue—A Structured  Narrative Review
content: Mental health disorders represent a growing public health burden in Southeast Asia, motivating interest in dietary approaches that may support mental well-being. This structured narrative review examines edible and medicinal mushrooms documented or consumed in the region across four outcome domains: mood, anxiety and stress; cognition; neuroprotection; and central or mental fatigue. Literature published up to June 2026 was identified using international and regional databases, ethnomycological sources and reference lists. Traditional uses primarily concern vitality and restoration rather than defined mental health conditions. Experimental evidence is largely derived from cell and rodent studies reporting antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, neurotrophic, neurotransmitter-modulating and gut microbiota-related effects. Human evidence comprises observational studies and a small number of trials, with mixed findings, particularly for Hericium erinaceus. Evidence from mushroom blends, isolated compounds and physical-endurance tests cannot be attributed directly to individual species or interpreted as evidence of reduced mental fatigue. Translation is limited by uncertain bioavailability, variable preparation methods and insufficient clinical and long-term safety data. These mushrooms remain candidates for research rather than established interventions. Authenticated, chemically characterised preparations and rigorous clinical trials are needed before mental health benefits can be established.
